paragraphs: This paper develops an ADHD detection model that combines brief changes in brain function with longer-term brain features. Its motivation is that existing graph-based approaches have given comparatively little attention to short-term functional reorganization. The proposed model therefore treats the sequence of changing brain activity patterns as useful information alongside the broader structure captured by a graph network.

The method first constructs a sequence of brain maps from short time windows. An encoder then represents both the state within those windows and the dependencies between them. A memory component connects current brain activity patterns with historical sequence patterns, giving the model a way to incorporate recurring temporal information. Separately, a graph neural network extracts longer-term features, which are combined with the short-term representation for detection.

Experiments on ADHD-200 and OpenNeuro-ds002424 report superior detection performance. These findings support the usefulness of combining information across timescales in the evaluated neuroimaging datasets, with memory providing an additional connection between present activity and earlier patterns.
icml-2026-adhd-disease-detection-based-o.tldr: The model combines short-term brain activity sequences, historical memory, and longer-term graph features to improve ADHD detection on two neuroimaging datasets.

paragraphs: Safety requirements differ across applications and can change over time, making a fixed judgment of acceptable behavior insufficient for some alignment tasks. This paper introduces the Configurable Safety Reward Model, or CSRM, to score responses according to supplied safety specifications. The goal is to support changing requirements while retaining the ability to provide useful training rewards.

CSRM is trained jointly for calibrated safety compliance and reward modeling. Its data augmentation targets particular configurations, encouraging the model to follow their instructions while preserving distinctions in the severity of violations. This connects sensitivity to the requested rules with sensitivity to conversational context, rather than treating every safety decision as an isolated, uniform classification.

The authors report improved generalization to unseen safety configurations and state-of-the-art results of 94.6% F1 on CoSApien and 75.8% F1 on DynaBench, without additional human annotation. Using CSRM for downstream alignment also improves the helpfulness–safety tradeoff against the evaluated baselines. The findings indicate that configurable reward judgments can translate into better aligned model behavior.
icml-2026-configurable-reward-model-for-.tldr: CSRM learns configurable safety rewards that generalize to unseen specifications and improve the helpfulness–safety tradeoff in downstream alignment.

paragraphs: Weak-to-strong generalization trains a more capable language model using examples produced by a weaker aligned model. This offers a way to transfer alignment without human feedback or a separately trained reward model. However, the weaker model's samples can carry noise and bias, making the quality of those training examples a central obstacle to reliable transfer.

The paper connects two ideas: implicit rewards expressed through log-likelihood ratios, and contrastive decoding, which compares model predictions during generation. It identifies a structural equivalence between them and builds ConG around that connection. ConG generates examples by contrasting a weak model before and after alignment, using the difference between those versions to obtain higher-quality samples for the stronger model.

Across different model families, the authors report consistent improvements in weak-to-strong generalization, including better denoising and robustness. The contribution is a method for improving the supervision supplied by a weak model through the generation process itself. These experiments support its applicability across the tested families, while the broader promise for more capable AI remains prospective.
icml-2026-contrastive-weak-to-strong-gen.tldr: ConG contrasts weak models before and after alignment to generate cleaner training examples for stronger models.

paragraphs: Most 3D assembly methods focus on finding the positions and orientations of available parts. CRAG broadens the task by jointly predicting those poses and generating a plausible complete object. The motivation is that understanding an object's overall shape can help determine how its pieces fit together, particularly when the observed parts leave the assembly ambiguous.

The two processes supply complementary information. Assembly contributes structural constraints from individual parts, helping guide shape generation. Generation supplies a holistic view of the object, helping resolve uncertainties about part placement. Because the method can synthesize geometry, it also addresses cases where some pieces are missing, rather than relying entirely on rearranging the geometry already supplied.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on objects with varied geometries, different numbers of parts, and missing pieces. These findings support treating generation and assembly as mutually useful tasks. The generated completion is described as plausible, so its role is to provide a coherent whole that informs assembly rather than establish that every missing detail has been recovered exactly.
icml-2026-crag-can-3d-generative-models-.tldr: CRAG jointly assembles 3D parts and generates complete shapes, using each process to improve the other.

paragraphs: DeltaEvolve addresses how a language-model-driven program search should remember earlier attempts. Keeping complete code histories can consume substantial context while burying useful algorithmic ideas in implementation details. The paper frames evolutionary search as an Expectation–Maximization process: the model proposes candidate programs, and evaluation feedback guides updates to the context used for subsequent proposals.

Within that framing, DeltaEvolve replaces full program histories with structured descriptions of changes between successive candidates. These semantic differences record what changed and how and why the changes affected performance. Because programs can often be decomposed into components, useful modifications may transfer to later candidates. A multilevel database and progressive disclosure further reduce the amount of information placed into the model's input.

Experiments across diverse scientific domains report better discovered solutions with lower token consumption than evolutionary agents using full-code histories. The results support the paper's central idea that search guidance benefits from representing the meaning and consequences of edits. Its efficiency improvement comes from making the accumulated history more informative as well as more compact.
icml-2026-deltaevolve-accelerating-scien.tldr: DeltaEvolve guides program evolution with structured explanations of useful code changes, finding better solutions with fewer tokens in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning behave differently when adapting multimodal models to convert PDFs into Markdown. The motivating observation is that supervised fine-tuning produces little improvement, particularly for difficult tables and formulas, whereas reinforcement learning delivers substantial overall gains. The authors examine what each training objective encourages the model to learn.

Their analysis finds complementary roles. Supervised fine-tuning mainly learns predictable document structure, such as the syntax needed to represent a table. Accurately reproducing the less predictable contents of individual cells remains harder. Reinforcement learning instead acts as a content refiner, using a holistic reward tied to final accuracy. The paper relates this difference to the theoretical properties of the two objective functions.

Based on that division of labor, the authors introduce a unified strategy intended to combine structural learning with content refinement. The findings suggest that document parsing benefits from matching training methods to different kinds of errors. They also explain why increasing post-training data alone may fail to capture the gains available from choosing complementary objectives.
icml-2026-dissecting-post-training-uncov.tldr: The study finds that supervised fine-tuning mainly teaches document structure while reinforcement learning improves content fidelity, motivating a combined training strategy.

paragraphs: Direct Preference Optimization aligns policies using preference comparisons without explicitly fitting a reward model. This paper studies what happens when those comparisons are distributed across users whose preferences differ. Such fragmentation changes optimization because local updates can pull in different directions, while communication limits how frequently participants can reconcile those differences.

The authors formulate personalized offline reinforcement learning with user-specific preference distributions and characterize the resulting global optimization problem. For federated training, they derive convergence rates that account for client drift, communication frequency, and preference heterogeneity. For decentralized training, they establish convergence over general communication graphs and explain how spectral connectivity—a property of how well the graph connects participants—affects both optimization speed and agreement.

Experiments on standard alignment benchmarks support the theoretical analysis and report robust, scalable performance for the proposed methods. The contribution connects distributed DPO's behavior to concrete features of the training system. In particular, it provides a framework for understanding how differing preferences and communication structure influence progress toward a shared optimization objective.
icml-2026-distributed-direct-preference-.tldr: The paper analyzes distributed DPO, showing how preference differences, communication frequency, and network connectivity affect convergence.

paragraphs: DRL-STAF forecasts multiple related time series while also estimating the hidden states associated with their next observations. The problem combines nonlinear observations, changing temporal behavior, and dependencies between sequences. Conventional deep learning can predict well without explicitly representing hidden states, while Hidden Markov Models provide those states but struggle with complex observation patterns and increasing scale.

The framework divides the work between neural networks and reinforcement learning. Neural networks model the nonlinear relationship between hidden states and observed values, while reinforcement learning estimates discrete hidden states. This reduces dependence on predefined transition structures and allows more flexible temporal dynamics. The approach also mitigates the rapid growth in state-space size encountered by typical multivariate Hidden Markov Model methods.

Across extensive experiments, DRL-STAF outperforms HMM variants, standalone deep models, and existing deep-learning–HMM hybrids in most cases, while producing reliable hidden-state estimates. That qualification matters: the reported advantage is broad but not universal. The findings support combining explicit state estimation with flexible prediction when both the next observation and its underlying state are useful outputs.
icml-2026-drl-staf-a-deep-reinforcement-.tldr: DRL-STAF combines neural forecasting with reinforcement-based hidden-state estimation, improving predictions in most evaluated cases.

paragraphs: Some retrieval tasks require a useful collection of items rather than one highly relevant result. Qualities such as diversity, coverage, and compatibility depend on relationships within the collection, so optimizing individual query–item matches does not fully capture the objective. This paper studies how to learn those collection-level properties while keeping results grounded in a fixed database.

R4T, or Retrieve-for-Train, uses reinforcement learning during training to make that objective available to a cheaper retriever. First, it trains a language model to produce multiple retrieval outputs using combined set-level rewards. Next, it uses that model to create training pairs reflecting the desired properties. Finally, a lightweight diffusion model learns the conditional distribution of these collections in embedding space.

Experiments on Polyvore and a music playlist dataset report better retrieval quality than strong baselines, together with an order-of-magnitude reduction in query-time fan-out latency. The approach separates learning a complex collection objective from serving requests. The expensive reinforcement-trained model supplies supervision, while the diffusion retriever carries that learned behavior into a more efficient retrieval process.
icml-2026-efficient-property-aligned-fan.tldr: R4T transfers collection-level retrieval objectives from an RL-trained language model into a lightweight diffusion retriever, improving quality and reducing query latency.

paragraphs: Training a language agent over long interactions requires determining which earlier actions contributed to an eventual outcome. That attribution becomes difficult when many decisions intervene between an action and its consequences. The paper identifies the resulting high variance in optimization as a major obstacle and introduces Hindsight Policy Optimization, or HPO, to obtain steadier learning signals.

HPO maps both the current policy distribution and a hindsight distribution into an intent space. In that space, semantically similar states and actions are grouped together. It then derives a policy-gradient learning signal from the Wasserstein distance between the two distributions. The comparison therefore operates on representations of intent, allowing similarities between interactions to contribute to the training signal.

The authors provide theoretical and empirical evidence that this semantic aggregation produces an estimator with bounded variance and improves policy performance stably. The significance lies in how the method converts hindsight into action-level guidance for long interactions. The stated result concerns bounded estimation variance and stable improvement; it does not require interpreting hindsight as a perfect explanation of each individual action's contribution.
icml-2026-from-outcomes-to-actions-lever.tldr: HPO compares current and hindsight behavior in an intent space to reduce learning-signal variance for long-horizon language agents.

paragraphs: HexGen-3 targets the cost of serving language models under production traffic with widely varying resource demands. Its central idea is to separate inference phases and operations so their resources can scale independently. This makes it possible to respond to the particular bottleneck of each component instead of adjusting the entire deployment as one unit.

The framework combines fully disaggregated inference with autoscaling across heterogeneous resources. A hierarchical scheduler jointly chooses resource allocation and parallelism settings for the resources currently provisioned. An autoscaling component then changes those resources as workloads fluctuate and triggers a new deployment schedule. Together, these mechanisms address both how to use an available resource pool and when that pool should change.

Compared with state-of-the-art serving systems, experiments report per-cost throughput improvements of up to 60%, averaging 46.5%, with static provisioning. Under dynamic workloads with autoscaling, improvements reach 78.3%, averaging 55.1%. These are efficiency gains measured relative to cost, supporting the value of coordinating fine-grained deployment decisions with changing resource availability.
icml-2026-hexgen-3-a-fully-disaggregated.tldr: HexGen-3 independently scales inference components and coordinates scheduling with autoscaling to improve LLM throughput per unit cost.

paragraphs: This paper makes Byte Pair Encoding tokenization incremental: as each byte arrives, the algorithm maintains the tokenization of the text received so far. It implements the standard merge procedure for a fixed set of BPE rules, allowing it to replace conventional BPE tokenization while supporting partial input in streaming language-model pipelines.

The main theoretical result bounds each byte's processing time by O(log² t) in the worst case, where t is the maximum token length. For an input of length n, total processing takes O(n log² t). The authors also introduce eager output, which emits a token once its boundary has been determined. Maintaining a prefix tokenization and deciding when tokens can be emitted are therefore both addressed.

Practical results include speedups of up to approximately three times over Hugging Face's tokenizers and significant latency reductions relative to tiktoken on pathological inputs. The findings combine worst-case computational guarantees with measured implementation benefits. The reported comparisons have distinct scopes: the tiktoken latency result specifically concerns difficult inputs, while the threefold figure is a maximum observed speedup.
icml-2026-incremental-bpe-tokenization-a.tldr: The algorithm incrementally maintains standard BPE tokenization with worst-case time guarantees and emits streaming tokens as their boundaries become determined.

paragraphs: KORE addresses two linked problems in updating a multimodal model: teaching it new facts and preserving what it already knows. Pretrained knowledge is static, but updating model parameters can interfere with earlier knowledge and cause catastrophic forgetting. The paper uses knowledge-oriented controls to shape both the information presented during learning and the direction of the parameter update.

The first stage automatically expands individual knowledge items into structured, comprehensive material to improve adaptation. The second represents previous knowledge through a covariance matrix of linear-layer activations. It initializes an adapter by projecting original weights into that matrix's null space, defining a fine-tuning direction intended to minimize interference with the represented prior knowledge.

Experiments with LLaVA-v1.5 at 7B and 13B and Qwen2.5-VL at 7B report superior new-knowledge injection and reduced catastrophic forgetting. The results support addressing adaptation and retention together through complementary controls. Structured knowledge helps the model acquire the update, while the activation-based constraint helps protect existing knowledge during that acquisition; the stated outcome is mitigation of forgetting rather than its complete elimination.
icml-2026-kore-enhancing-knowledge-injec.tldr: KORE combines structured knowledge preparation with constrained adapter initialization to improve new-knowledge learning while reducing forgetting.

paragraphs: LithoDreamer models computational lithography as a sequence of physical stages, from layout through mask and resist image to the image after development. The paper argues that existing models do not adequately capture this continuous process. Its world-model formulation represents how decisions and interventions influence successive stages, connecting process modeling with optimization.

The framework learns stage-specific latent spaces informed by physics, using feature changes between neighboring states. Within these spaces, it explores process interventions and predicts subsequent transitions. A contrastive variational optimization method compares latent differences between intervention paths while imposing evolution constraints. This is designed to guide physically consistent trajectories and interpretable intervention optimization without requiring continuous supervision.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance in both forward evolution and inverse planning. Forward evolution concerns predicting how the process develops, while inverse planning concerns selecting interventions to guide that development. The contribution is their integration within a multistage representation: the same model connects changes across the lithography pipeline with decisions about how to influence those changes.
icml-2026-lithodreamer-a-physics-informe.tldr: LithoDreamer models successive lithography stages in physics-informed latent spaces to improve process prediction and intervention planning.

paragraphs: Online reinforcement learning for language-model reasoning needs both varied exploration and sustained progress toward correct answers. This paper introduces IB-Score to evaluate that balance. Grounded in information bottleneck theory, the score relates diversity at individual reasoning steps to the mutual information those steps share with the correct answer, giving the tradeoff an explicit quantitative form.

Using this measure, the authors find that popular approaches such as GRPO, even with common regularization methods, do not consistently maintain balance during training. Their proposed IB-TPO makes IB-Score a fine-grained optimization objective. It also uses the score to guide tree-based sampling, then reuses the resulting tree to estimate IB-Score through Monte Carlo methods.

The sampling strategy produces 50% more trajectories under the same token budget. Across standard benchmarks, the authors report improvements of 2.9% to 3.6% over GRPO and better performance than other state-of-the-art online RL approaches. These findings connect training quality with sampling efficiency: the tree both supplies reasoning trajectories and supports estimation of the objective used to guide learning.
icml-2026-long-live-the-balance-informat.tldr: IB-TPO uses an information-based balance score and tree sampling to improve reasoning-model training and obtain more trajectories per token budget.

paragraphs: MM-Snowball studies how a multimodal model's initial visual mistake can spread through later conversation turns. The paper attributes this snowballing to increasing reliance on erroneous textual history as attention to the image weakens. Single-turn visual question-answering benchmarks cannot adequately expose this progression, motivating a benchmark designed to diagnose error propagation within dialogues.

Evaluations show that the benchmark challenges even advanced multimodal models and that existing mitigation methods developed for single-turn questions are ineffective in this setting. To address the problem, the authors introduce Conflict-Aware Visual Rectification, or CAVR. It requires no training and combines renewed visual grounding in the model's representations with corrections to output scores at the logit level.

The reported experiments give CAVR state-of-the-art performance. Its two mechanisms address related parts of the failure: how visual information is represented and how candidate outputs are weighted. The work makes conversational error accumulation an explicit evaluation target and shows that re-anchoring responses to visual evidence can mitigate the degradation observed across turns.
icml-2026-mm-snowball-evaluating-and-mit.tldr: MM-Snowball measures accumulating visual hallucinations in dialogue, and CAVR mitigates them by refreshing visual grounding and adjusting output scores.

paragraphs: Olaf-World addresses how to learn controllable video world models when action labels are scarce. Learning hidden action representations from passive video is promising, but those representations can become tied to particular scenes. The paper traces this problem to objectives that only compare information within individual clips, leaving action meanings unaligned across different contexts.

The proposed SeqΔ-REPA objective uses observable effects as a shared reference for unobserved actions. It aligns integrated latent actions with temporal feature differences produced by a frozen, self-supervised video encoder. This sequence-level comparison aims to give actions a more consistent meaning across contexts. Olaf-World incorporates the objective into a pipeline that pretrains action-conditioned world models on large-scale passive video.

Experiments report a more structured latent action space, stronger zero-shot action transfer, and more data-efficient adaptation to new control interfaces than state-of-the-art baselines. These results support using shared representations of action effects to improve transfer. The key contribution is an alignment signal across contexts, helping passive video supply reusable control information despite the absence of observed action labels.
icml-2026-olaf-world-orienting-latent-ac.tldr: Olaf-World aligns latent actions through their observable video effects to improve control transfer and adaptation from passive-video pretraining.

paragraphs: OServe addresses two kinds of variation in language-model serving workloads. Requests arriving together can have different compute and memory needs, and the mix of requests can change over time. A uniform deployment that remains fixed can therefore fit some workloads poorly. The paper proposes heterogeneous, flexible deployments to respond to both sources of variation.

The system has two complementary mechanisms. A workload-aware scheduling algorithm chooses heterogeneous model deployments using current workload characteristics. A workload-adaptive switching method then migrates deployments in response to predicted changes. The first determines an appropriate arrangement for present demand; the second provides a way to move between arrangements as the workload evolves.

Experiments using real-world traces show performance improvements of up to two times, averaging 1.5 times, compared with state-of-the-art serving systems. These findings support treating deployment configuration as a workload-dependent decision. The benefit comes from coordinating placement and adaptation with demand across devices and over time, with the reported maximum and average describing the evaluated traces rather than a fixed improvement for every request.
icml-2026-oserve-accelerating-llm-servin.tldr: OServe adapts heterogeneous model deployments to current and predicted workloads, reporting an average 1.5× serving performance improvement.

paragraphs: This paper studies private regression when each example contains public, non-sensitive features. Those features provide information that can be used without spending additional privacy budget. The authors focus on improving optimization in this setting, motivated by the observation that public feature matrices often have rapidly decaying spectra, meaning their structure is concentrated in relatively few directions.

Cond-DP modifies differentially private stochastic gradient descent using a conditioning matrix derived from public features. The matrix reshapes the optimization landscape to accelerate convergence. The framework includes ordinary DPSGD when the matrix is the identity, and the paper provides convergence guarantees for convex, strongly convex, and non-convex objectives. It also gives a construction that yields faster convergence for private linear regression without additional privacy cost.

Under label differential privacy, experiments across datasets and model architectures consistently outperform state-of-the-art baselines. The findings show how public structure can improve the utility of private learning. The privacy setting is central: the conditioning information comes from features already designated public, while the learning task retains its stated protection for sensitive information.
icml-2026-private-learning-with-public-f.tldr: Cond-DP uses public feature structure to accelerate private regression without additional privacy cost.

paragraphs: This paper studies cooperating service-system agents when some participants can maliciously manipulate exchanged parameters. Jobs have an affinity with servers that affects how they are processed. Each node learns a local policy through an actor–critic algorithm with linear function approximation and communicates with neighbors. The traffic-state space is inherently unbounded, creating a vulnerability that can destabilize both learning and queues.

The proposed algorithm makes the consensus process resilient to adversarial parameter manipulation. This matters because agreement between agents is part of how their local policies support a global objective. The authors prove traffic stability under mild assumptions and almost-sure convergence of cooperative policies to a bounded neighborhood of a stationary solution.

The convergence statement allows a bounded residual neighborhood; it does not claim exact arrival at a global optimum. Demonstrations cover semantic routing for language-model serving, distributed polling in cloud computing, and manufacturing logistics. Together, the analysis and examples connect protection of parameter exchange with operational stability in service systems whose workloads and server affinities influence control decisions.
icml-2026-secure-multi-agent-reinforceme.tldr: A resilient consensus-based learning algorithm limits malicious parameter interference and provides conditional guarantees for traffic stability and approximate policy convergence.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts language models save computation by using routers to activate selected experts at each layer. This paper investigates how those routing decisions affect safety. It identifies unsafe routes: configurations that can change an otherwise safe response into a harmful one. The finding makes the internal selection of experts an explicit subject for safety evaluation.

The authors introduce RoSais, a score measuring how important each layer's router is to safe behavior. They find that manipulating only routers with high scores can produce an unsafe route. They also develop F-SOUR, a fine-grained optimization framework that accounts for how routing varies across tokens and layers and for the sequential nature of input.

Across four representative MoE model families, F-SOUR reaches average attack success rates of 0.90 on JailbreakBench and 0.98 on AdvBench. These results demonstrate substantial vulnerability in the evaluated routing configurations. Safety-aware route disabling and router training are proposed as promising defensive directions, rather than established solutions, highlighting the potential value of incorporating routing behavior into future safeguards.
icml-2026-sparse-models-sparse-safety-un.tldr: The study finds routing configurations that undermine MoE model safety and identifies router-focused evaluation and defenses as important directions.

paragraphs: TreeCUA focuses on collecting better training trajectories for graphical-interface planning. Exploration across applications, desktops, and websites often revisits the same early steps before branching into different tasks. Representing those trajectories as a tree allows shared steps to be stored and replayed, reducing redundant exploration while retaining information about where alternative action sequences diverge.

The framework assigns collaborating agents to exploration, action verification, trajectory summarization, and quality evaluation. An adaptive exploration algorithm balances deeper trajectories, associated with greater difficulty, against broader exploration, associated with diversity. World knowledge guidance and global memory backtracking help avoid low-quality generation. These mechanisms combine trajectory quality control with more efficient reuse of explored interface states.

TreeCUA-DPO then uses information at neighboring branches to improve planning through preference optimization. The branch structure supplies reasoning evidence for distinguishing adjacent trajectories, giving the collected tree a second role in training. Experiments report significant improvements for TreeCUA and TreeCUA-DPO, while out-of-domain studies show strong generalization. The results support organizing exploration data around shared decisions and meaningful alternatives.
icml-2026-treecua-efficiently-scaling-gu.tldr: TreeCUA organizes verified GUI exploration into reusable trees and uses branch comparisons to improve computer-use planning.

paragraphs: Test-time prompt tuning adapts a vision–language model using several augmented versions of a test image. This paper revisits that procedure and interprets its optimization as learning from labels generated by the model itself. That perspective makes the reliability of those pseudo labels a central concern and motivates aligning how predictions are combined during adaptation and final inference.

The proposed self-ensembling strategy adaptively gives the original image greater emphasis than its augmented views when constructing pseudo labels. USE applies the same strategy at inference, keeping the two stages consistent while still exploiting the augmentations. The self-ensembling component can also operate independently as a lightweight adaptation method that requires no optimization.

Across multiple datasets, the authors report that self-ensembling and USE outperform their respective counterparts. Self-ensembling also produces consistent gains when added to existing test-time adaptation methods. The findings support treating prediction aggregation as part of adaptation design: how original and augmented views are combined affects both the supervision used for tuning and the final prediction.
icml-2026-use-a-unified-self-ensembling-.tldr: USE consistently combines original and augmented image predictions during prompt tuning and inference to improve test-time adaptation.

paragraphs: Predicting a cell's response to a genetic perturbation requires detecting a small changing signal within much larger amounts of unchanged gene-expression information. This paper argues that the imbalance can undermine learned representations in two ways: they may mix perturbation-specific effects with invariant structure, or suppress the sparse effects needed for prediction.

PerturbedVAE explicitly separates perturbation-specific information from the dominant invariant component and recovers causal representations to use that information for prediction. The authors also analyze identifiability, characterizing conditions under which sparse perturbation effects can be reliably recovered. This conditional analysis connects the framework's design to the circumstances in which the desired separation can be established.

On a widely used benchmark, PerturbedVAE achieves state-of-the-art results across multiple evaluation settings, with significant gains for out-of-distribution predictions involving combinations of perturbations. It also reveals interpretable perturbation-response programs. The results support preserving small but consequential changes during representation learning, while the theory makes clear that reliable recovery of those effects depends on the characterized conditions.
icml-2026-what-makes-a-representation-go.tldr: PerturbedVAE separates sparse perturbation effects from dominant unchanged expression patterns to improve cellular-response prediction and interpretation.

paragraphs: Z-Erase targets the removal of unwanted concepts from text-to-image models that process text and image tokens in one shared stream. Because those tokens use shared parameters, applying erasure methods developed for other architectures typically causes image generation to collapse. The paper develops a framework tailored to this coupling between language and image processing.

Its first component disentangles the update process, enabling existing concept-erasure methods to operate within the single-stream architecture while maintaining stable generation. A second component uses Lagrangian-guided adaptive modulation to balance removing the targeted concept against preserving other model behavior. This casts erasure as a constrained tradeoff, rather than optimizing concept removal without accounting for preservation.

The authors prove that Z-Erase can converge to a Pareto stationary point, a qualified optimization result concerning the competing objectives. Experiments report that it overcomes generation collapse and achieves state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of tasks. The contribution combines an architecture-specific update framework with an adaptive mechanism for managing the erasure–preservation balance.
icml-2026-z-erase-enabling-concept-erasu.tldr: Z-Erase adapts concept removal to single-stream diffusion transformers while balancing erasure with preservation of stable image generation.
